title: Are you in the room? A framework for sortition and representation
text:
A thesis submitted for the degree of Bachelor of Commerce (Honours) at Monash University, Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics.

Abstract
Sortition, the random selection of individuals to form panels, has seen a renaissance in recent years, as more and more institutions realise the value of direct community and stakeholder input in deliberation and policymaking. These panels have proven to be massively beneficial in terms of improving the quality of outcomes reached, increasing public trust and engagement, and creating more inclusive and representative processes. However, there are still many challenges to overcome in order to ensure that these panels are truly representative and selected effectively. This thesis aims to evaluate current sortition methods and community representation processes, as well as to investigate how sampling biases and algorithmic design can impact panel representativeness. By investigating these factors, we can develop a greater understanding of existing tools and procedures, how they work, how they fall short, and what it would mean for them to be more representative. This enabled the creation of a diagnostic tool (“Intersection Inspector”), for use by practitioners to make the process more transparent, and to assess and improve the representativeness of selected sortition panels.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Background
In a social landscape where the public is growing progressively disillusioned with its representation in politics (Landemore 2026), it is important to consider ways in which we can foster more inclusive decision-making practices. One way of achieving this is using sortition to create panels that are more representative of the population for political discussions and deliberations. Adopted recently by an increasing number of institutions, including the Parisian (“Paris creates a permanent Citizens’ Council” 2021), Irish (Walsh and Elkink 2021), and British Columbian (Ward 2008) governments, sortition as a part of democratic process is gaining traction. As a result, the need for fair and representative methods of building panels is only growing, and progress is being made in improving the structure of selective algorithms. However, there are still many challenges to overcome in order to ensure that these panels consistently achieve the level of representation that they envision. And there remains little procedure on measuring representativeness beyond the “surface” marginal level of demographics.
Sortition is a method of selection that uses random sampling to create panels that should be descriptively representative of a population. It has been used in various contexts, reaching as far back as ancient Athens (where it was how jurors were selected), and now into modern times for citizens’ assemblies. The idea is that by randomly selecting individuals from the population, we can create panels that are more representative and inclusive than those selected through traditional methods, like elections or open-ended surveys. Due to its random nature, sortition also reduces dominance by elites or highly engaged groups, enabling broader participation across social classes (Giuliani 2025), making it more likely that decisions are in the relevant population’s best interest.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 The representation problem
One of the main roadblocks in sortition is ensuring that the selection process is transparent and fair, and that the panels are truly representative of the population in terms of demographics and perspectives. But this raises the questions of what it means to be fair, what it means to be representative, and how these look from a systematic perspective. A fair lottery is not, by itself, proof of a representative outcome – it answers whether everyone had a reasonable chance of being chosen, not whether the people who actually get chosen reflect the community they are meant to stand in for. This thesis is concerned less with whether the process was fair, and more with a plainer question underneath it: who actually ends up in the room?
As a process, sortition can be broken down into four stages: 1) defining the population and traits of interest, 2) requesting expressions of interest from a random subset of the population, 3) feeding respondents into a sortition algorithm, and 4) panel selection and engagement for deliberation. Notably, there is currently no rigorous evaluation of representation achieved before a process is run. Additionally, each of these steps has the potential to introduce bias, impacting the representativeness of the panel. As such, it is crucial to measure how the level of representativeness (or potential representativeness) flows through each stage, and to understand how different factors may affect it.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Evolution of sortition methods
Sortition methods have been evolving over time. Prior to algorithmic means, panel selection was carried out through simple self-selection (response to survey/advertising) and proportional sampling to meet panel size requirements. As sortition began to grow more robust, the Legacy techniques (Flanigan et al. 2021) started surfacing – these saw panels put together through simple choosing of respondents who met the most required “category” condition at any given moment, and would continue iterating until the required marginal counts were present in the selected panel. This led to situations of extreme selection likelihoods, if minorities existed – as members were selected indiscriminately of implied likelihood, meaning there were situations where an individual would potentially be selected 0% of the time. To counteract this, the more systematic algorithm “MaxiMin” was implemented (Baharav and Flanigan 2024); seeking not only to meet panel quotas, but to raise the lowest individual’s selection likelihood, with the aim of eliminating the 0% selection case, in order to improve representativeness. This, however, now presented the risk of likelihood manipulation, as selection was based more directly on the combination of all category responses given by an individual, rather than pure counts needed for the panel to be filled. As a result, the inverse function “MiniMax” was employed to reduce extreme cases on the other end – eliminating the 100% selection chance case by minimising maximal selection likelihood of any given individual, providing an approach that was more resistant and robust to coercion, but simultaneously reintroducing the potential 0% likelihood problem. Though robustness itself lies beyond the scope of this paper’s aims, it is important to note the existence of MiniMax as an approach to the sortition problem, as it impacted further algorithmic development.
More recently, and of direct relevance to the current study, further iterations of MiniMax and MaxiMin, in the forms of “LexiMin” (Flanigan et al. 2021) and “Goldilocks” (Baharav and Flanigan 2024), were established. These present more generally practical outcomes, with the former being used in industry at present. LexiMin takes the idea of MaxiMin and repeats it for every individual sequentially, maximising all individuals’ likelihoods, rather than just those who sit at the absolute bottom. Thus, raising the selection likelihood floor for the participant pool overall. It is, however, like MaxiMin, vulnerable to manipulation (which remains beyond the scope of this paper) – leading into the development of the Goldilocks algorithm solution. Goldilocks aims to simultaneously raise the selection likelihood floor (eliminating the 0% selection chance and improving representativeness), as well as lower the ceiling (eliminating the 100% selection case and making the process more robust against manipulation). A tool for Goldilocks’ use is in development at the time of the writing of this paper, and is expected to be made publicly available in the near future. As such, it will not be used for the current study, but may present an opportunity for further research.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 This thesis
Notably, all of these algorithms only focus on optimising for maximal selection likelihoods as their sole objective functions. This means that in its discovery and construction of feasible panels, the existing LexiMin algorithm may be prone to distortion of intersections and intersectional association trends present within population distributions. This presents a massive risk for the validity of representation achieved by panels output by the algorithm – the extent and reasoning of which will be explored further in the paper.
Additionally, there is limited literature on the visualisations of the outputs of these algorithms. This presents a great opportunity to demistify LexiMin and sortition as a process, improving transparency for practitioners, facilitators, participants, and broader community stakeholders alike. The comparative visualisation methods and tools also allow a general comparison to be made between any selected group and any broader sample it is pulled from, with any algorithm or selection process. This could be massively useful as a mechanism for quick sanity checks of panel configurations, and as a way for practitioners to evaluate the validity of panels before engaging in deliberation.

Thesis structure
The remainder of this thesis is structured as follows: Chapter 2 provides a literature review of the existing research on sortition and representation, and identifies gaps in the current knowledge. Chapter 3 outlines the simulation-based methodology used to evaluate panel representativeness, including how differential survey non-response is modelled alongside an equal-chance baseline, and the statistical tests used to assess whether a panel’s joint category distribution preserves the association present in the sample it was drawn from. Chapter 4 presents the results of the analysis, showing near-total intersectional association distortion in selected panels, well beyond what a random-sampling benchmark would produce. Chapter 5 introduces “Intersection Inspector”, a tool developed in response to those results to help practitioners assess panel representativeness directly. Chapter 6 concludes by proposing a framework and recommendations for practitioners, discussing the limitations of this thesis, suggesting directions for future research, and reflecting on what genuine representation demands beyond marginal fairness – namely, keeping sight of who the process is meant to represent, and whether it actually does.

text: 2.1 Representation and sortition

title: 2  Literature review
text:
What does it mean to be representative?
Every sortition selection method shares the same basic aim: a panel that is fair and representative of the population. But what does that actually mean?
Fairness means the selection process is transparent, unbiased and inclusive – everyone should have an equal chance of being chosen, regardless of their background or demography. In practice, this comes down to minimising the gap in selection likelihood across the pool, typically achieved by introducing randomness into the process (Flanigan et al. 2021a); without it, selection bias creeps in implicitly.
Representativeness, meanwhile, is about whether the selected panel actually reflects the demographics and perspectives of the population it was drawn from – diverse, inclusive, and populated by people from the range of backgrounds the process set out to capture. This can be checked directly, by comparing a panel’s demographic makeup against the population’s.
Approaching it procedurally, the sortition process can be thought of in four stages:

Defining the population and traits of interest
Sampling from a random subset of the population (through survey or other outreach)
Panel selection (through algorithmic means or other method)
Panel evaluation, confirmation and engagement

Each step is a chance for bias to creep in and representativeness to suffer, which is why it matters to evaluate representativeness (or potential representativeness) at every stage, not just the end.
If the population and the traits of interest are poorly defined, for instance, the selection process may fail to capture the group’s actual diversity, leaving the panel less representative. This is a real challenge in itself: most population descriptions, as discussed above, record demographic characteristics separately rather than capturing how they intersect, which is central to representativeness. Addressing that gap properly would mean wading into broader data collection and storage practices, which is beyond this thesis’s scope – but it is worth keeping in mind that representation goes beyond the margins.
The same applies to survey response: if certain groups are less likely to respond, they end up underrepresented in the pool of potential panelists before a panel is even assembled. If a survey of an area that is 60% women somehow drew no female respondents at all, representativeness would already be violated well before selection begins. Cases like this raise the question of how to account for non-response bias, and whether visualisation can help show the gap between the respondent pool and the population – which is part of what this thesis sets out to do.

title: 2  Literature review
text:
2.2 Panel selection

Problem definition
Suppose there is a pool of individuals numbered 1 to n, from which we want to choose a panel of size k. Let K be the set of all feasible panels – any group of k individuals satisfying the required constraints, which generally take the form of quotas.
Quotas specify a desired count, or range of counts, for individuals in a given trait class (e.g. 20-22 males, or 15-17 rural), tied to whichever demographics a project has deemed important to represent. The core goal of sortition, then, is to build a panel that meets those quota constraints equitably, robustly, and in a way that genuinely represents the population it was drawn from.


Existing methods

Non-algorithmic/self-selection
This is the simplest method of panel selection: individuals are simply allowed to self-select, for example by advertising the opportunity and taking sign-ups on a first-come, first-served basis. These methods tend not to produce representative panels, for two reasons. First, they invite self-selection bias – involvement depends on exposure rather than random chance, and the people who put their hand up are more likely to already hold formed opinions, ahead of ever joining the panel. Second, they tend toward lower engagement, since there is no guarantee of reaching a particular level of exposure in the first place.


LEGACY heuristic (Flanigan et al. 2021a; Sortition Foundation 2024)
Already an improvement on non-algorithmic methods, the LEGACY selection heuristic builds a panel by selecting respondents one at a time until it is full. At each step, it calculates a “need” value to find the trait currently furthest from its desired count, then picks a random individual who has that trait. If selecting someone would push a trait past its upper quota, everyone else with that trait is removed from the pool before the next pick. This repeats until the panel is complete, or the process runs out of eligible individuals and restarts. LEGACY satisfies the basic requirement of meeting quotas, but it does not maximise representativeness: it ignores each individual’s actual selection likelihood (which, in extreme cases, can end up at 0%) and makes no attempt to minimise the maximum deviation from an equal chance of selection. For a time, this was the Sortition Foundation’s own method of panel selection, implemented in their GroupSelect tool, before the algorithmic fairness methods below were developed and adopted.


MaxiMin (Flanigan et al. 2021b) and MiniMax (Baharav and Flanigan 2024)
This shortcoming is addressed by the first two algorithmic sortition methods, MaxiMin and MiniMax, which tackle the problem in opposite ways. MaxiMin generates potential panels and selection probabilities, then sets out to maximise the minimum selection probability across the pool. This reduces the chance of any individual never being picked, improving fairness, but makes the method vulnerable to manipulation – someone who misreports belonging to an under-represented quota group can inflate their own odds. MiniMax instead minimises the maximum selection probability, making selection more robust against manipulation, but at the cost of fairness, since the risk of a 0% selection chance returns.


LexiMin (Flanigan et al. 2021a)
LexiMin – short for lexicographic minimisation – works similarly to MaxiMin, but resolves ties sequentially rather than stopping at the single minimum. It first identifies whoever has the lowest selection chance and maximises that, then moves to the next-lowest, and so on, until every individual’s selection probability has been addressed and made as equal as possible across participants. This gives everyone the highest chance of selection achievable without disadvantaging someone already prioritised – but, like MaxiMin, it inherits a vulnerability to manipulation.


Goldilocks (Baharav and Flanigan 2024)
This brings us to the current gold standard: the aptly-named Goldilocks algorithm. Goldilocks simultaneously maximises minimum selection probabilities (for fairness) and minimises maximum selection probabilities (for robustness), aiming for a “best of both worlds” balance between MaxiMin and MiniMax. The motivation is concrete rather than abstract: MaxiMin places no ceiling on how high an individual’s selection probability can climb, so a participant who misreports their trait membership to appear under-represented can disproportionately inflate their own odds. By capping the maximum selection probability, as MiniMax does, Goldilocks limits the payoff from that kind of manipulation while still prioritising the lowest probabilities enough to preserve most of MaxiMin’s fairness guarantees – a selection rule that is simultaneously hard to game and reasonably fair.



LexiMin approach (Flanigan et al. 2021a)
Rather than committing to a single panel immediately, LexiMin constructs a probability distribution over the full set of feasible panels K, assigning each panel S \in K a non-negative probability p_S that sums to one across the set. An individual’s overall selection chance is then the sum of the probabilities of every panel that includes them. Sorting these chances from smallest to largest, LexiMin proceeds lexicographically: it maximises the smallest probability first, then – holding that value fixed – maximises the second-smallest, and so on until every individual has been addressed.


Formal representation
This process can be expressed formally. Let p_S denote the probability assigned to panel S, which must be non-negative and sum to one across every feasible panel in K,

p_S \ge 0, \qquad \sum_{S \in K} p_S = 1.

The resulting selection probability for an individual i is then the sum of the probabilities of every feasible panel containing them,

\pi_i(p) = \sum_{S \in K,\ i \in S} p_S,

giving the full vector of individual selection probabilities across the population,

\pi(p) = (\pi_1(p), \pi_2(p), \ldots, \pi_n(p)).

Sorting this vector from smallest to largest,

\pi_{(1)}(p) \le \pi_{(2)}(p) \le \ldots \le \pi_{(n)}(p),

LexiMin chooses the distribution p that maximises this sorted vector in lexicographic order – that is, the smallest entry first, then the second-smallest subject to the first remaining maximised, and so on down the sorted vector.


Algorithm
In practice, this lexicographic maximisation runs as a sequence of steps: every feasible panel in K is listed alongside every possible probability distribution over those panels, and for each candidate distribution the resulting selection probability \pi_i(p) is computed for every individual i and sorted smallest to largest, \pi_{(1)}(p) \le \pi_{(2)}(p) \le \ldots \le \pi_{(n)}(p), as above. Only the distribution (or distributions) that maximise the smallest probability \pi_{(1)}(p) are retained; if several remain tied, this narrows further to those that also maximise the second-smallest, \pi_{(2)}(p), and so on, resolving ties one probability at a time until a single distribution remains. A final panel is then sampled from it.


Logic
At its core, LexiMin is a fairness rule: it prioritises whoever has the lowest chance of selection, improves their odds first, then works through the next-lowest probabilities until no further improvement is possible without disadvantaging someone already prioritised. The result is selection probabilities as equal as possible across the population, within the panel’s quota constraints.


Visualisation methods
To evaluate the representativeness of selected panels, this thesis draws on a range of visualisation methods that compare a panel’s trait distribution against the sample it was drawn from, and surface any discrepancies or bias in the selection process. Useful options include bar charts, mosaic plots, double decker plots, UpSet plots, and parallel coordinate plots.
Bar charts are the starting point: simple illustrative graphs of trait densities that give a rough sense of how the population and samples break down, setting expectations for the more detailed visualisations that follow. From there, mosaic or double decker plots show the proportion of demographic traits selected onto panels. UpSet plots (Conway et al. 2017) are useful for showcasing the intersections present in generated panels, linking demographic variables visually alongside frequency counts of how often each combination occurs.


Discussion
This approach is effective at making selection probabilities as equal as possible, which helps make sortition fairer by reducing situations where specific individuals are disadvantaged. It does not, however, provide any way to impose joint trait requirements on subsets of the population – something that may be necessary for accurate representation of community groups. That gap can undermine representativeness as a goal, given the motivation for sortitioned panels in the first place: filling a room with individuals who accurately and descriptively reflect a community’s population diversity and characteristics.


New investigation
Across this literature, the common thread is that algorithmic effort has gone almost entirely into optimising the fairness and robustness of the selection mechanism – how equal selection probabilities are, and how resistant they are to manipulation – rather than validating the outcome that mechanism produces. A panel satisfying every fairness and robustness guarantee an algorithm offers is not thereby guaranteed to represent the population it was drawn from well; these are related but distinct properties, and the literature so far has focused heavily on the former at the expense of the latter.
One specific way this gap shows up: no algorithmic technique surveyed here stratifies for combinations of demographic traits in its decision-making – each instead affects individual selection chances purely through quotas set on each trait at the margin. This is a real limitation, since it means the selection process may fail to capture the group’s actual diversity, leaving a less representative panel. In some situations – side-panels built for specific subgroups, or communities with known intersectional minorities of interest – ensuring specific intersectional combinations are included may be necessary for genuine representation. This gap is generally patched in practice by bringing in “specialist speakers” during deliberation (Redman and Carson n.d.), but that is a different kind of inclusion than being part of the panel and its decision-making directly.
Notably, this gap is rarely argued for directly; it is simply left unaddressed. The implicit assumption running through this literature appears to be that satisfying marginal quotas is enough – that selecting individuals to hit the right counts for each trait independently will, through the randomness built into the selection mechanism, naturally produce a panel whose combinations of traits are also reasonably representative, without this needing to be checked or enforced directly. None of the algorithmic methods reviewed above test whether this actually holds, and the literature more broadly does not appear to examine it either.
This thesis treats that assumption as an open empirical question rather than a safe default. The simulations that follow test how much intersectional inclusion happens naturally under current methods, and establish a way to measure how much intersectionality and association survives the selection process.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.1 Research aims
This thesis set out to assess whether current algorithmic methods achieve representative panels, diagnose whether a sample’s association trends survive the sortition process, demystify sortition selection to improve its transparency, and provide a framework for more informed, standardised practitioner decisions.
Underlying these aims is a more basic question: what does it mean for a panel to be “good” at representation, and are current methods actually achieving it? That breaks down further. Are algorithms like LexiMin performing as well as they could? How well do intersectional associations and trends survive selection, and therefore how representative is panel composition? And how much can differing survey response rates and other sampling-level issues bias representativeness, beyond whatever the algorithm itself contributes?

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.2 Research design

Simulation design
This thesis investigates how data complexity and construction affect algorithmic performance. To test this, two population of simple intersectional complexity (two variables) with varying associations (independent and associated) was simulated. The findings should generalise to cases with more categories, and are expected to be more severe there, since the intersectional matrix only grows in dimension while panel size stays fixed. The categories used – age (18-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+) and tenure status (rent, own, other) – were chosen to mirror demographic variables commonly used for sortition in practice. Combining these two variables produced the four simulated sample/respondent datasets used for panel selection.


Population, slice, sample and panel: procedure and definitions
Every simulated dataset in this thesis moves through the same four stages, with terms kept deliberately consistent throughout to avoid ambiguity – “sample” in particular is used loosely, and inconsistently, across much of the sortition literature.

Population: the full simulated universe of individuals (n_{\text{total}} = 100{,}000), generated from a specified joint probability array over the category variables. This represents the entire community eligible for selection, with marginal and joint (intersectional) distributions known exactly, since they were specified directly in the data-generating process.
Slice: a simple random sample, without replacement, of 10% of the population, drawn before any response behaviour is simulated – representing the group actually invited to take part (e.g. mailed a survey), sometimes called the invited pool elsewhere. Because it is drawn uniformly at random, the slice’s composition deviates from the population’s only through ordinary sampling variability, not systematic bias.
Sample: the subset of the slice who actually respond, determined by an independent Bernoulli trial for each invited individual under one of the response-rate cases described below. This is the realised pool available for panel selection – also called the respondent pool or survey sample elsewhere – and the benchmark every panel’s representativeness is compared against, since it, not the full population, is what any practical algorithm actually draws from.
Panel: a fixed-size subset of k members drawn from the sample by a selection algorithm (LexiMin, via Panelot, in current practice) subject to quota constraints on each category level’s permitted count – the final body that would convene to deliberate, and the unit whose representativeness this thesis is ultimately concerned with.









Figure 3.1: The four stages of the simulation pipeline: population, slice, sample and panel.





Each stage can introduce its own departure from the population’s true composition: the slice through ordinary sampling variability, the sample through differential response rates, and the panel through the selection algorithm’s own quota mechanism (Section 3.3). Distinguishing these stages explicitly makes it possible to attribute any observed distortion in a final panel to a specific stage of the pipeline, rather than to sortition “in general”.


Two-variable illustrative example: age and tenure
To illustrate the general procedure concretely at a minimal scale, this thesis builds a simple two-variable example using only age and tenure. Age is denoted A, taking one of L_A = 5 ordered levels a \in \{1, \dots, 5\} (18-34 through 65+), and tenure is denoted T, taking one of L_T = 3 levels t \in \{1, \dots, 3\} (Rent, Own, Other). Marginal probability vectors were defined for each variable,

\mathbf{p}_A = \left(p_{A_1}, \dots, p_{A_5}\right), \qquad \mathbf{p}_T = \left(p_{T_1}, p_{T_2}, p_{T_3}\right), \qquad \sum_{a=1}^{5} p_{A_a} = 1, \qquad \sum_{t=1}^{3} p_{T_t} = 1,

with \mathbf p_A = (0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.25, 0.15), a mild skew toward the upper-middle age brackets, and \mathbf p_T = (0.30, 0.50, 0.20), a moderate skew toward home ownership. Both the independent and associated populations below use these same marginal targets, so any difference between them is attributable solely to the association introduced, not to a difference in either variable’s marginal distribution.
An independent population (sim_data2) was generated by taking the outer product of these two marginals to form a joint probability array,

P^{(0)}(a, t) \;=\; p_{A_a} \, p_{T_t}, \qquad \mathbf{P}^{(0)} \;=\; \mathbf{p}_A \mathbf{p}_T^\top \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{5 \times 3},

a 5 \times 3 matrix whose row sums equal \mathbf p_A and column sums equal \mathbf p_T by construction, so that A \perp T. This array was flattened into a probability vector and cell counts were drawn from a single multinomial trial before being expanded into individual-level records, as described in full below.
A second, associated population (sim_data2_cov) uses the same marginal targets but deliberately introduces a negative association between age and renting, via an ordinal score for age,

s(a) = \frac{a - 1}{5 - 1} \in [0, 1],

running from 0 for the youngest bracket to 1 for the oldest, which was used to seed the independent array \mathbf P^{(0)} with an exponential adjustment factor targeting only the “Rent” level of tenure,

\tilde{P}(a, t) \;=\; P^{(0)}(a, t) \cdot \exp\!\Big(-\alpha \, s(a) \cdot \mathbb{1}[t = \text{Rent}]\Big), \qquad \alpha = 1.2,

scaling down the probability of renting by a factor of e^{-\alpha s(a)} that grows with age, while leaving owning and other tenure unchanged. Because this adjustment only touches the “Rent” column, the row and column sums of \tilde{\mathbf P} no longer equal \mathbf p_A and \mathbf p_T, so the array was rescaled through iterative proportional fitting (raking) to restore the age and tenure marginals exactly to their specified targets. Initialising P^{(0)}_{\text{rake}} = \tilde P, each raking iteration r = 0, 1, 2, \dots performs two rescaling passes,

P^{(r + 1/2)}(a, t) \;=\; P^{(r)}_{\text{rake}}(a, t) \cdot \frac{p_{A_a}}{\sum_{t'} P^{(r)}_{\text{rake}}(a, t')}, \qquad
P^{(r+1)}_{\text{rake}}(a, t) \;=\; P^{(r+1/2)}(a, t) \cdot \frac{p_{T_t}}{\sum_{a'} P^{(r+1/2)}(a', t)},

first rescaling every row to sum to p_{A_a}, then every column to sum to p_{T_t}. Repeating this pair of passes for R = 100 iterations (well past convergence for a 5 \times 3 table) yields the raked array P^\star, satisfying

\sum_{t} P^\star(a, t) = p_{A_a} \; \text{ for all } a, \qquad \sum_{a} P^\star(a, t) = p_{T_t} \; \text{ for all } t,

to numerical tolerance, while retaining the negative age-renting association introduced by the exponential seeding step – raking restores the specified marginals while preserving the association the adjustment introduced.
Both populations were sampled the same way, differing only in which array was used. The relevant array (\mathbf P^{(0)} for the independent case, or the raked P^\star for the associated case) was flattened into a probability vector \mathbf p^\star \in \mathbb R^{15} (age varying fastest), and cell counts were drawn from a single multinomial trial,

(n_1, \dots, n_{15}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\!\left(n_{\text{total}}, \, \mathbf p^\star\right), \qquad n_{\text{total}} = 100{,}000,

with each cell j, corresponding to one (a, t) combination, expanded into n_j individual-level records sharing that age and tenure. Comparing the two resulting populations demonstrates the core logic of the simulation framework in its simplest form: a chi-squared test of association between age and tenure is non-significant in the independent population but highly significant in the associated population, with the conditional probability of renting falling steadily from around 44% among 18-34 year olds to around 18% among those aged 65 and over, even though both populations share identical marginal distributions for age and tenure individually. This confirms the seeding-and-raking procedure successfully introduces a targeted association without disturbing the overall marginal proportions, and sets up a direct test of whether the selection algorithm preserves intersection structure beyond the purely marginal level.
As is standard practice, a random slice of the population (10%) is taken to serve as the survey sample, from which responses are drawn. Concretely, from a population of n_{\text{total}} individuals, a survey sample \mathcal{S} of size n_{\mathcal S} = \lfloor 0.10 \, n_{\text{total}} \rceil (so n_{\mathcal S} = 10{,}000 for the two-variable example, drawn uniformly at random without replacement) is taken as the invited pool, before any response behaviour is simulated. Whether each invited individual i \in \mathcal S actually responds is then modelled as an independent Bernoulli trial,

R_i \;\overset{\text{ind.}}{\sim}\; \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),

where the response probability \pi_i is assigned according to one of two cases: an independent case, and an age-covaried case mirroring the age-renting association introduced at the population level above.
In the independent case, every invited individual is equally likely to respond regardless of their trait profile,

\pi_i = \pi_0, \qquad \pi_0 = 0.30,

a baseline against which the effects of differential response can be compared; a chi-squared test confirms no significant association between A and R here, as expected. In the age-covaried case, response likelihood increases with age, reusing the same ordinal score s(a) defined above,

\pi_i = \pi_1 \exp\!\big(\alpha_R \, s(a_i)\big), \qquad \pi_1 = 0.20, \quad \alpha_R = 1.0,

so that the response rate rises from around 20% among the youngest bracket to over 50% among the oldest, and the association between A and R is now highly significant.


From survey sample to panel
Applying both response cases to both populations produces four respondent-pool files – sim_data2_ind_eq.csv, sim_data2_ind_ass.csv, sim_data2_cov_eq.csv and sim_data2_cov_ass.csv – each containing only the individuals who actually responded under that population/response-case combination, with their age and tenure. These names follow the same <ind|cov>_<eq|ass> convention used for the lottery files below, so a file name alone identifies both the population and response case it came from. Each respondent pool is, in the terminology above, a sample: the realised pool a panel can actually be drawn from. Each file was then passed to Panelot’s LexiMin algorithm, along with quota constraints on the permitted count of each age bracket and tenure category (based on the population’s marginal distributions, with ±1 individual slack allowed for the 18-34 and 65+ brackets, which would otherwise require non-integer solutions), to enumerate every feasible panel of k = 50 members – yielding four lottery files (lottery_ind_eq.csv, lottery_ind_ass.csv, lottery_cov_eq.csv and lottery_cov_ass.csv) evaluated in Section 3.3.


Validating the simulation: numerical summary
Alongside the mosaic plots used throughout this chapter to compare the age x tenure population, slice and respondent sample visually, each simulated dataset is also checked numerically, to confirm the data-generating process behaved as intended before any downstream panel evaluation. Two quantities recur throughout this checking, and resurface in a more formal role in the panel-level association testing described in Section 3.3:

A chi-squared test of independence, applied to the 5 \times 3 age-by-tenure contingency table, confirms whether the intended association (or lack of it) was actually realised in a given dataset. A non-significant result (p > 0.05) for the independent population (sim_data2), alongside a significant result for the associated population (sim_data2_cov), is the expected pattern – a sanity check on the simulation code, not a substantive finding in its own right.
Marginal proportion tables (prop.table() applied to the age and tenure frequency tables) confirm that each variable’s marginal distribution matches its specified target (\mathbf p_A or \mathbf p_T) to within sampling error, at both the population and sample level. This matters particularly for the associated population, where raking is specifically designed to restore exact marginal targets despite the association-inducing adjustment applied beforehand.

Later, when panels themselves are evaluated (Section 3.3), the same chi-squared logic is extended into a three-way log-linear homogeneity test, and supplemented with Cramer’s V as an effect-size measure, so a panel’s divergence from its sample can be judged on both statistical significance and practical magnitude, not significance alone.


Method limitations and caveats
The response rates used for the age x tenure pipeline – a 30% baseline in the independent case, rising to over 50% in the age-covaried case – are considerably higher than response rates typically reported for real-world sortition, where response to a civic lottery invitation is often below 10%. This was deliberate, not an oversight: response rates that low, applied to a 10,000-person slice, would in some conditions leave too few respondents in individual age-by-tenure cells (there are 15) to reliably assess an algorithm’s ability to satisfy quotas or preserve intersectional structure at k = 50 – the algorithm would be data-starved regardless of its own effectiveness. Elevating the response rate ensured enough data richness to isolate the algorithm’s own behaviour as the object of study. One consequence: any representativeness issues identified here should be read as a conservative, best-case estimate. At the lower response rates typical of practice, the same mechanisms – differential non-response, quota-constrained selection leaving the joint age-tenure distribution unconstrained – would have less data to work with and correspondingly more room to produce poorly representative panels, not less.
Every association deliberately introduced in the age x tenure pipeline – the negative age-renting association at the population level (\alpha = 1.2) and the age-response association at the sampling level (\alpha_R = 1.0) – was controlled by a single exponential strength parameter, fixed at a moderate-to-strong value chosen to make each association clearly visible in a mosaic plot and reliably detectable by a chi-squared test at this thesis’s sample sizes. These values were not derived from any specific real-world dataset, and the algorithm’s representativeness or association-preservation performance is unlikely to degrade uniformly with the strength of the underlying association: a weaker real-world association might be preserved adequately by a process that fails on the stronger one simulated here, or, conversely, a subtler association could be more easily disrupted if it rests on fewer affected individuals. Because this simulation uses a small number of fixed association strengths rather than a systematic sweep, the panel-level results in Section 4.3 should be read as showing that association-preservation failures of this kind are possible and can be severe at the strength simulated, not as a precise, generalisable estimate of their magnitude across the full range of strengths that might occur in practice.
A further question is what a panel’s divergence from its sample actually shows, not just how large it is. Panelot’s quota constraints come from each category’s population marginal distribution, not from the marginals actually seen in the survey sample a panel is drawn from and compared against (Section 3.3). So a panel built to satisfy population-based quotas could, in principle, diverge from its sample on exactly the margins those quotas target. This could happen simply because the sample’s own composition has drifted from the population’s, whether through ordinary sampling variability or, more importantly, through differential non-response.
This turns out not to be a real concern for the test actually driving this thesis’s headline results. The panel-versus-sample test behind Table 4.2’s “significantly different” flag (Section 3.3, which gives this test’s full notation) compares a panel against the rest of its sample using a three-way age-by-tenure-by-group interaction term in a log-linear model. Its null model already allows age and tenure to vary separately by group, so the panel and the rest of the sample are free to have completely different age marginals and completely different tenure marginals without that alone counting as significant. Only a genuine difference in the age-tenure association, separate from each group’s own marginals, can trigger the test. Panelot’s quotas are marginal-only, not joint, so population-based marginal correction has no way to show up as a false association-divergence flag here. The very thing this concern describes is exactly what the test rules out by design. (The same is not true of the standalone Cramer’s V figures reported alongside this test – for example, the sample- and panel-level Cramer’s V in Table 4.2 and Table 4.3. Those are computed from each table on its own, rather than as a group comparison, so they do stay sensitive to marginal drift and should be read with that in mind.)
The equal-chance and age-associated lottery files offer a second, empirical reason to reach the same conclusion. Under equal-chance response, the survey sample’s age marginal already matches the population’s closely (Figure 4.2, Figure 4.3), leaving barely any population-versus-sample gap for population-based quotas to correct. Yet Table 4.2 shows the equal-chance files (lottery_cov_eq.csv, lottery_ind_eq.csv) flagged as different at least as often as the age-associated ones, where the sample’s marginal has genuinely drifted from the population’s (Figure 4.4, Figure 4.5). If population correction were driving the divergence, equal-chance panels should have been flagged less often, not equally or more. Both the test’s design and this comparison point the same way. The near-total divergence documented here reflects the quota mechanism leaving the joint age-tenure distribution unconstrained, exactly the effect this chapter sets out to measure, rather than any population-versus-sample drift.
This question – panel-versus-population quotas, compared against a panel-versus-sample test – also explains why the survey sample, rather than the population, is used as the benchmark throughout this thesis, despite being an imperfect proxy for the population it represents. In practice, a practitioner running a real sortition process has no access to the population’s joint age-tenure distribution (or any other intersectional combination) to check a panel against – population-level data at the intersectional level is rarely collected or published, which is precisely the gap this thesis is concerned with (Chapter 2). Quotas are set from population marginals for the same reason, since those are typically the only population-level statistics available (e.g. census tables). The survey sample is therefore the best source of joint, intersectional information a practitioner actually has, and comparing a panel against it – as done throughout Section 3.3 and Section 4.3 – is the most direct representativeness test that could be run in practice, not merely a convenience adopted for this simulation.


Visualisation methods
The choice of visualisation follows directly from the nature of the data. The variables of interest – age brackets, tenure status, and the other demographic categories used for sortition – are categorical rather than continuous, and the central question is how they intersect, not how any one is distributed in isolation. Many standard tools are a poor fit for this: scatterplots and histograms are built for continuous data; a bar chart or pie chart can show one categorical variable’s marginal distribution but not how two or more co-occur (Section 4.1 demonstrates this concretely); and a bar chart faceted or grouped by a second variable becomes difficult to read once cell counts are uneven – precisely this thesis’s situation – because bar heights are not naturally comparable in the way proportional tile areas are. The mosaic plot, by contrast, is designed specifically for this kind of cross-classified categorical structure, representing both marginal distributions and their joint, intersectional distribution within a single figure, which is why it is the primary visualisation tool used throughout this thesis.
A mosaic plot visualises the joint distribution of two or more categorical variables: each combination of categories is a rectangular tile, its area proportional to the number (or proportion) of observations sharing that combination. This suits the question this thesis is concerned with – not just whether individual categories are represented in the right proportions (a bar chart could already answer that), but whether particular combinations of categories are over- or under-represented relative to what population demographics would predict, and whether the variables are independent. Because tile area scales with both variables at once, a mosaic plot reveals an association between categorical variables – a departure from independence – that would not be visible from either variable’s marginal distribution alone.
To make later plots easy to interpret, the simplest form of a mosaic plot is shown below:









This example plot examines just two variables: favourite fruit and favourite ice cream flavour. The example data set generated 25 individuals per marginal option (50 total), then shuffled them randomly to produce independent intersectional combinations. The width of each top-level bar is proportional to that category’s marginal share of the data (here, the number preferring each fruit), while the height of the coloured segments stacked within a bar is proportional to the conditional proportion of the fill variable (here, the proportion preferring each ice cream flavour, given a fruit preference). Because fruit and ice cream preference were shuffled independently, the two fruit bars split at close to the same width, confirming visually that the variables carry no association: knowing someone’s favourite fruit gives no information about their favourite ice cream flavour. Where fill proportions differ noticeably from one bar to the next, that indicates an association – precisely the pattern distinguishing the independent and associated age-tenure populations introduced above.
Throughout the rest of this thesis, this same convention – categories on the x-axis with width proportional to marginal share, and a second variable shown via fill colour with segment height proportional to conditional proportion – is used for the core population, slice and sample comparisons, with age brackets on the x-axis and tenure as fill.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.3 Panel-level association evaluation

Panel generation and representation
With the two-variable populations, survey samples and respondent pools constructed above, the final stage of the pipeline draws an actual panel from the respondent pool. This was done using Panelot, a sortition tool that selects panels of a fixed size k (here k = 50) subject to quota constraints on each variable’s margin independently – a minimum and maximum permitted count for every age bracket and tenure category, specified in a categories.csv file. Rather than a single fixed panel, Panelot’s output, lottery.csv, enumerates every feasible panel its selection algorithm discovered, together with the exact probability q_j panel j would be returned were the lottery run, so \sum_j q_j = 1 across the J discovered panels. Each row lists the pool identifiers of the k = 50 selected respondents.
A deliberate feature of this quota structure is that it constrains the age and tenure margins of a panel separately, with no quota placed on their joint (intersectional) distribution. Two panels can therefore satisfy identical quotas – the same count of 18-34 year olds, the same count of renters – while differing substantially in which individuals combine which age with which tenure. This asymmetry between marginal and joint representativeness motivates the association-level evaluation developed below.
Four lottery files were generated in this way, covering every combination of the two populations (independent and associated) and the two response-rate cases (equal-chance and age-associated) introduced previously: lottery_ind_eq.csv, lottery_ind_ass.csv, lottery_cov_eq.csv and lottery_cov_ass.csv.


Linking panels to the survey sample
Each panel’s members are identified only by pool identifier in lottery.csv, so their age and tenure values were recovered by joining back onto the respondent-pool CSV originally supplied to Panelot (the same file written by csv_helper.R, e.g. sim_data2_cov_eq.csv). This respondent pool – the people who were invited to respond and actually did so – is referred to throughout as the survey sample, and serves as the benchmark against which every panel’s composition is compared.


Within-panel association test
For each discovered panel j, a 5 \times 3 contingency table of age against tenure was constructed from its k = 50 members, and a chi-squared test of independence applied to assess whether age and tenure appear related within that panel alone. With only 50 observations spread across 15 cells, several expected cell counts fall below the conventional rule-of-thumb minimum of five, so a Monte Carlo approximation to the null distribution (simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000 resamples) replaced the standard asymptotic chi-squared reference distribution.


Panel-versus-sample homogeneity test
The within-panel test alone cannot establish whether a panel’s association differs from the survey sample’s – a panel could show a significant association purely because the sample itself does. To test this directly, each panel j was compared against the remainder of the survey sample via a three-way log-linear model. Writing G for a binary group indicator (panel member vs. not), a Poisson model was fitted to the cell counts of the 5 \times 3 \times 2 Age \times Tenure \times G table, first without the three-way interaction,

\log \mathbb{E}[\text{Freq}] = \beta_0 + \beta_A^{(a)} + \beta_T^{(t)} + \beta_G^{(g)} + \beta_{AT}^{(a,t)} + \beta_{AG}^{(a,g)} + \beta_{TG}^{(t,g)},

and then with it,

\log \mathbb{E}[\text{Freq}] = \beta_0 + \beta_A^{(a)} + \beta_T^{(t)} + \beta_G^{(g)} + \beta_{AT}^{(a,t)} + \beta_{AG}^{(a,g)} + \beta_{TG}^{(t,g)} + \beta_{ATG}^{(a,t,g)}.

A likelihood-ratio test between these two nested models isolates the three-way interaction term \beta_{ATG}: a significant result indicates that the age-tenure association differs between panel members and the rest of the sample, i.e. that panel j’s intersectional composition is not merely a smaller, noisier version of the sample’s, but systematically different from it.


Multiple testing
Because every panel discovered for a given lottery file is tested this way – several hundred to several thousand panels per file – the homogeneity test was repeated many times over. Results are reported at an uncorrected threshold of \alpha = 0.05 throughout.


Benchmark against random sampling
A panel of only 50 members is itself a small sample, so some disagreement with the full survey sample’s association is expected from sampling variability alone, independent of anything specific to Panelot’s mechanism. To separate a genuine quota-constrained-selection effect from this baseline noise, the same homogeneity test was applied to 500 simple random samples of size 50, drawn without quota constraints from the same survey sample. If panels were no more divergent from the sample than equivalently sized random draws, the proportion flagged as significantly different should resemble the proportion of random samples flagged – approximately \alpha under the null.


Effect size
Alongside each test, Cramer’s V,

V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2 / n}{\min(r - 1, \, c - 1)}},

was computed from the within-panel contingency table (r = 5 age brackets, c = 3 tenure categories) to express the strength, rather than merely the statistical significance, of the association detected within each panel.

title: 4  Results
text:
4.1 The problem with current visualisations
Before turning to this thesis’s main results, it is worth demonstrating directly why mosaic plots – rather than the pie charts (or equivalent bar charts) that commonly accompany a sample or panel’s reported composition in current sortition practice – are used throughout this chapter, rather than simply asserting it (Chapter 3).
Figure 4.1: Age and tenure marginal proportions for the independent population (top) and associated population (bottom). Each population’s age pie chart (left) and tenure pie chart (right) are visually indistinguishable from the other population’s, despite the two populations differing sharply in their underlying age-tenure association.
Figure 4.1 uses this thesis’s own independent and associated populations (sim_data2, sim_data2_cov) to make the point concrete. The two populations were constructed, by design, to share near-identical age and tenure marginal distributions – the raking procedure used to build the associated population exists specifically to restore the independent population’s marginals while retaining the age-renting association introduced beforehand (Chapter 3) – so the largest gap between the two populations’ marginal proportions, across any single age bracket or tenure category, is only 0.02 percentage points, fully attributable to multinomial sampling noise rather than anything deliberately different between them. Unsurprisingly, each population’s age and tenure pie charts are visually indistinguishable from the other’s.
Yet the two populations are not the same: the associated population carries a genuine, and statistically detectable (Table 4.1), negative association between age and renting, while the independent population has none at all. A pie chart – or a bar chart, which encodes exactly the same single-variable information in a different shape – has no visual channel available to show this: it can only display one categorical variable’s marginal distribution at a time, so two variables each need their own, entirely separate chart, and nothing in either chart can reveal how the two co-occur. A practitioner shown only the pie charts in Figure 4.1 would have no way of telling the independent and associated populations apart, despite one holding a materially different – and, as Section 4.3 goes on to show, selection-relevant – relationship between age and tenure than the other. The mosaic plots used throughout the remainder of this chapter (Chapter 3) exist specifically to close this gap, representing both variables’ marginal distributions and their joint, intersectional distribution within a single figure.

Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.3 trace each population’s age-tenure structure across the three pipeline stages under the equal-chance response case. Both populations skew towards upper-middle age and a higher frequency of homeownership than other categories. In Figure 4.2, there is no visible association between age and tenure at any stage – the probability of any age-tenure intersection is explained purely by the margins – and this independence, along with each category’s relative proportions, is preserved essentially unchanged from the full population through the slice to the equal-chance respondents. In Figure 4.3, by contrast, a negative association between age and renting is visible at every stage: the proportion of renters among the youngest bracket is noticeably higher than among the oldest. This pipeline, too, carries its association and relative proportions through from population to slice to equal-chance respondents largely unchanged, confirming that neither random slicing nor equal-chance response meaningfully disturbs either population’s underlying age-tenure structure.

Figure 4.4 and Figure 4.5 repeat the same three-stage pipeline, but with response likelihood now rising with age rather than being equal across brackets. This shows that an association between age and response probability – entirely independent of any association between age and tenure in the underlying population – is sufficient on its own to shift the overall age composition, and therefore the intersections present, in the final respondent sample. Comparing Figure 4.5 against Figure 4.3 shows this age-skew compounding with the associated population’s existing negative age-renting relationship, rather than replacing it: respondents under age-associated response are weighted even further towards the older, lower-renting end of the distribution than either the equal-chance respondents or the slice itself.

Table 4.2 summarises the results across all four lottery files. In the associated population, the survey sample itself retains a clearly detectable age-tenure association (Cramer’s V around 0.13), consistent with the negative age-renting relationship built into the population design. In the independent population, by contrast, the sample-level association is negligible and statistically indistinguishable from zero (both p > 0.5), exactly as expected given no association was introduced between age and tenure at the population level.
Despite this contrast in the underlying samples, the proportion of panels flagged as holding a significantly different association from their sample is strikingly similar – and strikingly high – across all four files: between 99.8% and 100%. In other words, essentially every panel Panelot could possibly return, under either population structure and either response-rate case, exhibits an age-tenure relationship detectably different from the sample it was drawn from – including in the independent population, where there is no true association for a panel to even distort.
Splitting this range apart by file shows little further structure: the two equal-chance lotteries (lottery_cov_eq.csv, lottery_ind_eq.csv) each flag 100% of their feasible panels, while the two age-associated lotteries fall only fractionally short, at 99.93% and 99.77% respectively – despite these two files containing roughly twice as many feasible panels (2981 and 3483, against 1867 and 1516), and therefore more opportunities for an occasional panel to be drawn that does not diverge from its sample. In other words, the proportion flagged is already saturated at or near its ceiling in all four files, regardless of whether the underlying population carries a genuine age-tenure association (cov) or none at all (ind), and regardless of whether response probability is equal across ages or skewed toward older respondents. Neither factor moves the result in a way that a difference of a few feasible panels out of several thousand cannot already explain – the distortion identified here looks like a property of the quota mechanism itself, not of any particular population or response structure it happens to be applied to.

Figure 4.6 makes concrete what the aggregate figures above describe in summary. The survey sample (left) shows the smooth, gradually strengthening relationship between age and renting built into the associated population. The panel (right) satisfies the same marginal quotas on age and tenure, but its age-tenure combinations are considerably more blocky and uneven – several age brackets are almost entirely one tenure category, a pattern far more extreme than the sample-level relationship it was ostensibly drawn to represent.
